title: Cleverbridge breach exposes customers' card numbers — and the CVV codes that should never have been stored
summary: Hackers stole payment card numbers, expiry dates and CVV security codes from software e-commerce platform Cleverbridge, which detected the intrusion on November 4 but only began notifying customers on November 20. The company has not explained how attackers obtained codes that payment rules forbid storing.
content:
Software e-commerce platform Cleverbridge has confirmed that hackers stole customers' payment card numbers, expiry dates and card security codes, in a breach that raises serious questions about how data that should never have been stored ended up in attackers' hands.

The Germany-headquartered company, which processes online payments and manages subscriptions for software businesses in more than 240 countries, said it detected unauthorised activity on its platform on November 4. It cut off the intruders' access the same day and brought its systems back online, but a subsequent investigation established that payment card information had been copied from its systems.

Cleverbridge began notifying affected customers on November 20, more than two weeks after the intrusion was discovered. The company has not said how many people are affected, which of its business customers' shoppers were hit, how the attackers got in, or how long they were inside its systems before detection.

What was taken is, on the available evidence, the worst possible combination for online fraud. According to a notification letter seen by The Register, the stolen information includes "your card number, expiry date, card security code (CVV/CVC), and contact details", along with email addresses, billing addresses and phone numbers. A separate notification reviewed by BleepingComputer listed the card details but said no other personal data had been accessed — a discrepancy the company has not explained. Cleverbridge says there is no indication that account passwords were compromised.

The stolen security codes are the most troubling part of the incident, and the part Cleverbridge has so far failed to explain. The three- or four-digit CVV is the code printed on a card that helps verify online purchases, and the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard — the rulebook the card networks require merchants and payment processors to follow — explicitly prohibits storing it after a transaction is authorised, even in encrypted form. That leaves only two possibilities, and Cleverbridge has confirmed neither: either the codes were improperly retained on its systems, or the attackers intercepted them while payments were being processed. As [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/11/23/cleverbridge-admits-attackers-stole-customers-credit-card-and-cvv-numbers-yep-you-read-that-right/5311573) reported, the company has not explained how the attackers obtained the codes, whether they were retained after transactions, or whether they were captured in transit.

The scale of the exposure is difficult to gauge, partly because Cleverbridge is a company most shoppers never knowingly deal with. It handles the business of selling software online — payments, subscriptions, tax compliance — on behalf of other firms, so customers may have typed their card details into a Cleverbridge checkout without ever seeing the company's name. Its client roster includes well-known names in enterprise IT and security, among them Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Parallels, Plesk, Sony, Malwarebytes and Sophos. None of those companies has been named as affected, and Cleverbridge has not said which of its clients' customers were caught up in the breach.

A ransomware group calling itself N0n has claimed responsibility for the attack and reportedly leaked the stolen data on its dark web leak site, according to Infosecurity Magazine. Cleverbridge, for its part, has confirmed that the incident was not a ransomware attack and that none of its systems were encrypted — a statement that rules out one common scenario without explaining how the intruders got in or what they did once inside.

For anyone who receives a notification, the advice is straightforward and urgent. Cleverbridge recommends checking card statements carefully and telling the card issuer immediately about any transaction that is not recognised. Because the stolen combination — card number, expiry date and CVV — is exactly what is needed to attempt purchases online without ever touching the physical card, banks may need to replace affected cards rather than simply monitor them. Affected customers are being offered 24 months of free credit monitoring and fraud assistance through TransUnion's Cyberscout service.

The incident also exposes a wider problem with how breaches are disclosed. Cleverbridge's public incident page says little about exactly what was stolen, directing customers to their individual notification letters instead — and those letters, as the two published copies show, do not agree with each other. The company waited 16 days between detecting the intrusion and starting to notify customers, a delay it has not justified, and it has still not disclosed the number of victims, the attack method, or the duration of the intrusion.

Regulators and the card networks are likely to want answers to the CVV question above all. If a payment processor was holding security codes it was forbidden to store, the breach is not only a security failure but a compliance one, with consequences that could extend well beyond the customers whose cards were exposed. Until Cleverbridge explains how the codes were accessible at all, its customers — and the software companies that trusted it with their checkouts — are left guessing how much damage has been done.

The breach comes in a month already crowded with major cyber incidents, from the [first fully autonomous AI cyberattack reported by Google](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/google-first-fully-autonomous-ai-cyberattack-november-2026) to the [Java4Shell flaw that governments warned could let hackers take over servers](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/java4shell-flaw-governments-warn-systems-open-hackers-november-2026). What sets the Cleverbridge case apart is not its scale, which remains unknown, but the nature of what was taken: the one piece of card data that the industry's own rules say should never be there to steal.
